sections.html:
Lee County's seat, Tupelo, lies in northeast Mississippi about midway between Memphis and Birmingham. With 37,923 residents in 2020, Tupelo ranks seventh in Mississippi by population and acts as the shopping, banking and industrial center for its region. Interstate 22 and U.S. Route 78 serve its 51 square miles.

The census found 17,102 housing units, 9.5 percent of them vacant. Houses that owners lived in were rarely empty (homeowner vacancy was 1.5 percent), but 13.3 percent of rentals were. A seller answers to two offices here. City hall covers permits and code, while county government covers property tax.

Storms are part of local memory. Tornadoes hit Tupelo on May 8, 2008, April 28, 2014 and May 2, 2021, the last one striking the northwest side of downtown. An inspector who sees a patched roof or a repaired wall will ask about it, and a seller holding repair paperwork can answer in a minute.

Permits, building, planning and code enforcement all run through Development Services, upstairs at City Hall, 71 East Troy Street. It will not approve a permit unless the applicant has a current recorded deed. Reach permitting staff at 662-841-6510 or permits@tupeloms.gov.

Keeping a property within the city's ordinances and Development Code is the owner's job, and Code Enforcement assists. If you receive a violation letter or citation, resolve it with that office, because fines can follow otherwise. The city also publishes a rental inspection checklist and property maintenance standards, and the Building Division runs a Blight and Demolition Program.

  • Search for open violations before listing, because a buyer's due diligence can find them.
  • For a rental, ask Permitting how the rental inspection process works.
  • Collect permits for past work. Every application needs a recorded deed.

Some neighborhoods sit inside historic and design overlay districts, including the downtown historic district and the Fairpark redevelopment district, each with its own standards. Planning is the office to ask before exterior changes near downtown.

sections.h2: Lee County property tax and homestead
sections.html:
Lee County mails the bill for the prior assessment year, and it must be paid on or before February 1. A house its owner lives in is Class I, counted at 10 percent of true value, and all other real property is Class II at 15 percent. Revaluation happens at least once every four years.

Homestead filings go to the Tax Assessor from January 1 through April 1, and the paperwork generally includes a recorded warranty deed, Social Security numbers and the cost of the home. The basic tier gives a credit of up to $300. Owners 65 or older or totally disabled owe nothing on the first $7,500 of assessed value.

The exemption follows the owner, which means a buyer has to own the house and live in it as a primary residence on January 1, and the deed must be on file at the Chancery Clerk before January 7.

Check for delinquent taxes early. The Tax Collector's office posts a final day to pay real property taxes ahead of the August tax sale. After a lien sale, the owner can still pay the taxes with interest of 1.5 percent per month through the Chancery Clerk, within two years. If you owe anything, request a payoff figure and settle it out of the sale proceeds so the buyer receives a clear title.

Section 89-1-503 of the Mississippi Code has the seller deliver a written property condition disclosure statement before title moves. If the buyer gets it only after making an offer, the buyer may cancel in writing within three days of hand delivery or five of mailing.

Describe known problems plainly, including past storm repairs, roof work and any water in the crawl space or basement. Honest answers protect you and tend to speed up a sale, because the buyer has fewer surprises to negotiate over.

sections.h2: Your options for selling in Tupelo
sections.html:
Tupelo owners tend to choose from three routes: an agent listing, a sale to an investor, or a direct as-is sale to a cash buyer. Listing fits a house in good repair and a seller with time. Cash often suits storm damage, code violations, tax trouble or a multi-heir estate.

Whichever you pick, begin with a title search by an attorney or title company, which shows liens, unpaid taxes and whether the seller holds legal title. After an offer is accepted, the usual steps follow: payoff of any mortgage or tax balance from the proceeds, signing of the deed, and recording by the Chancery Clerk. Bring photo identification, repair and permit records, and a mortgage payoff figure if you have one.

Cash Home Buyers speaks with Tupelo sellers about as-is purchases and explains the terms in writing before you decide, so you can compare them against listing.

sections.h2: Preparing a storm-worn house for buyers
sections.html: If your Tupelo house has taken wind or hail, a patched ceiling or a roof repair, put the story on paper before anyone asks. List the date of each repair, who did the work, and whether a permit or insurance claim was involved. Photos of the work in progress help, and so do receipts. A buyer who sees a clear record tends to worry less, and an investor who sees none will lower the offer to cover the unknown. Either way, you stay in control of the conversation.

Pick a closing date with the tax calendar in mind. A house that closes in the weeks before January 1 changes who gets that year's homestead exemption, and a balance due before the August tax sale is easier to settle early than to chase late. If a lease is running, line the date up with the end of the lease. If the house is vacant, a shorter timeline saves you the monthly cost of insurance and utilities on an empty property.

sections.h2: Selling an estate or inherited house
sections.html: Several heirs mean extra steps. Everyone with a legal interest has to agree, and the person signing needs authority to do so. Before you accept an offer, confirm that taxes are current, that no code letter is outstanding, and that a recorded deed is available, since a new owner will need one for any permit. A cash buyer can close without asking the heirs to pay for repairs, which is why this route comes up often for inherited property.

faqs.q: Do I need a recorded deed to pull a permit in Tupelo?
faqs.a: Yes. The city approves no permit without a current recorded deed, and every application needs a completed form plus the deed.

faqs.q: When are Lee County property taxes due?
faqs.a: On or before February 1 for property assessed the preceding year. If February 1 falls on a weekend, payment the following Monday is accepted.

faqs.q: Who do I call about property taxes in Lee County?
faqs.a: The Tax Collector is at 662-432-2200 and the Tax Assessor at 662-432-2700. The Homestead Office is at 662-432-2706.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Tupelo house that has code violations?
faqs.a: Yes. The letter or citation still has to be resolved with Code Enforcement, and open issues can show up in a buyer's inspection, though a cash buyer will price the problem in.

faqs.q: How long can I redeem a house sold at a tax sale in Lee County?
faqs.a: You have two years from the purchase date, paying the taxes plus 1.5 percent monthly interest through the Chancery Clerk.
